lede: The 204 notes questions ask you to meet a precise writing goal. Use the goal to choose relevant facts and the intended relationship, then verify the answer against the notes. The reported goal-only model result is not a guarantee for students.

steps.title: Read the goal first
steps.text: It is the last line of the notes: “The student wants to …”. Name what it asks for in two or three words: a similarity, the aim of the study, an introduction for a new audience.

steps.title: Read the four choices
steps.text: Ask which choices meet the goal. Then verify the selected facts and relationships against the notes.

steps.title: Drop accurate choices that do a different job
steps.text: College Board’s own explanations say “this choice doesn’t [the goal’s verb] …” for about 439 of the 612 wrong choices. Wrong choices are usually true; they just do something else.

steps.title: Verify the facts and scope
steps.text: Check that the surviving choice accurately states the notes and satisfies the whole goal. A goal-only model result does not guarantee factual accuracy on another question.

goalsIntro: The goal’s verb and its object tell you what the right choice must contain. Counts are of the 204 notes questions.

goals.right: Names both things and what they share. “Both”, “similar”, “like”, “also”, “same”, “share”, “as well” or “likewise” is in 14 of 17 right answers and 6 of 51 wrong ones.
goals.trap: A true fact about only one of the two.

goals.right: Sets the two against each other in one sentence (whereas, while, unlike, but, than): 22 of 24 right answers.
goals.trap: Facts about each side, but no contrast between them.

goals.goal: Present the aim of a study
goals.right: Says what the researchers wanted to find out (“to determine”, “wanted to learn”): 6 of 9 right answers, 1 of 27 wrong ones.
goals.trap: How the study was done, or what it found.

goals.goal: Introduce something to an unfamiliar audience
goals.right: Explains who or what the thing is, not just its name.
goals.trap: A name dropped with no explanation, as if the reader already knows it.

goals.right: A broad statement about a kind of thing, with few specific names (1.4 capitalized names per right answer against 2.0 per wrong one).
The quotation that does the job the goal names. 9 of the 18 wrong choices also quote someone, so check what the quote says.
goals.trap: A real quotation on a different point.

traps: The goal’s first verb, across the 204: emphasize 65, present 20, explain 16, specify 13, describe 12. Each one names the job; the wrong choices do a neighboring job.
Watch for “only one of the two” on similarity and contrast goals, and for “how” instead of “why” on aim goals.
caveat: The goal-only test was run by Claude on all 204 notes questions with the notes removed, then scored against College Board’s key. The tell counts are pattern matches on the choices, and the “doesn’t” count is a pattern match on College Board’s explanations, so both are close, not exact.
